title: Committed climate warming
problem: The paper challenges the widespread misinterpretation that substantial future warming is unavoidable due to climate inertia from past emissions, a perception that wrongly shifts policy focus from aggressive mitigation towards adaptation.
method: The paper proposes reinterpreting climate commitment based on a zero-emissions scenario, arguing that because future warming is not inevitable from past emissions, aggressive mitigation to eliminate future emissions should be the highest priority to avoid dangerous climate change.
task: The task is to re-evaluate the concept of committed climate warming, arguing that future temperature change is determined by future emissions rather than climate system inertia from past emissions, thereby challenging the inevitability of future warming.
innovation: This paper challenges the notion of unavoidable global warming by arguing that future warming is driven by continued emissions, not past ones, as eliminating carbon dioxide emissions would lead to the rapid stabilization of global temperatures.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Figure 1 | Two representations of climate commitment. Constant-composition commitment (red line) represents the future warming associated with current atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations, and zero-emissions commitment (blue line) represents the warming commitment from past carbon dioxide emissions (simulated here by the UVic Earth System Climate Model; refs 6 and 9). Also shown are the constant-composition commitments simulated by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change fourth assessment report (IPCC AR4) models (orange line, multimodel mean; yellow shading, range spanned by models)², the zero-emissions commitment simulated by the HadCM3LC and BERN2.5CC models (grey lines; refs 7 and 8, respectively) and historical temperature data (black line). Constant atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations lead to continued warming for many centuries, whereas the elimination of carbon dioxide emissions leads to approximately stable or decreasing global temperature.
